title: Evolution and speciation
summary: What evolution is, the evidence for it from molecules, selective breeding and anatomy, and how new species arise when populations become reproductively isolated.

keyterms.definition: Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations.
Comparison of DNA, RNA or protein sequences: closely related species have fewer differences, indicating common ancestry.
Humans choosing organisms with desired traits to breed (artificial selection), producing large heritable changes in domesticated species over relatively few generations.
A structure with the same basic anatomy in different species, inherited from a common ancestor, though it may now have different functions.
Limb with a single proximal bone, two distal bones, carpals/tarsals and five digits; homologous in amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
A structure with a similar function in different species that evolved independently, not from a common ancestor, e.g. wings of birds and insects.
Independent evolution of similar features in unrelated groups due to similar selection pressures; the origin of analogous structures.
The formation of new species by splitting of a pre-existing species.
Separation that prevents gene flow between populations so they cannot interbreed.
Different selection pressures acting on separated populations, causing them to diverge.
Speciation in which populations are separated by a geographical barrier.
Speciation within the same geographical area, due to behavioural or temporal isolation or polyploidy.
Rapid diversification of one ancestral species into many species adapted to different niches.
Inability of interspecific hybrids to produce gametes because chromosomes cannot pair in meiosis, e.g. the mule.
Having more than two sets of chromosomes; can cause abrupt speciation in plants, often after hybridization.

questions.prompt: Which is the best definition of evolution?
options: Change in the heritable characteristics of a population
Changes acquired by an individual during its lifetime
The development of an organism from embryo to adult
Improvement of organisms towards perfection
questions.explanation: Evolution applies to populations and only to heritable traits. Acquired characteristics are not inherited, and evolution has no goal.

questions.statement: An individual organism can evolve during its lifetime.
questions.explanation: Evolution is change in a population over generations. Individuals may change (e.g. by growth or learning), but these changes are not inherited.

questions.prompt: Why do differences in amino acid sequences of a protein provide evidence for evolution?
options: Proteins in all species are identical
Species that look different always have the same sequences
The number of differences correlates with how long ago species shared a common ancestor
Amino acid sequences change only in response to the environment
questions.explanation: Mutations accumulate gradually, so closely related species have few differences, consistent with descent from common ancestors.

questions.text: Breeding domesticated animals and crops with desirable traits is called ___ breeding.
questions.explanation: Selective breeding shows that heritable characteristics can change greatly in a short time, e.g. varieties of cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli from wild mustard.

questions.statement: The forelimbs of humans, bats, whales and birds are homologous structures.
questions.explanation: They share the pentadactyl limb plan inherited from a common ancestor, even though they are used for grasping, flying in bats, swimming and flying in birds.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct example.

pairs.right: Many dog breeds from wolf ancestors

questions.explanation: Homologous structures share ancestry; analogous ones only share function; selective breeding shows rapid evolutionary change.

questions.prompt: What is the origin of analogous structures?
options: Inheritance from a recent common ancestor
Convergent evolution under similar selection pressures
Selective breeding by humans
Use and disuse of organs during an animal's life
questions.explanation: Unrelated organisms facing similar demands (e.g. flight) can independently evolve similar structures with different underlying anatomy.

questions.prompt: Order the bones of a pentadactyl limb from the shoulder (or hip) outwards.
items: Two bones (radius and ulna or tibia and fibula)
Group of wrist or ankle bones
questions.explanation: This same pattern appears in all tetrapod limbs, which is why the pentadactyl limb is evidence of common ancestry.

questions.text: Similar features evolving independently in unrelated groups is called ___ evolution.
questions.explanation: Convergent evolution produces analogous structures, which can mislead classification based on appearance alone.

questions.prompt: Why is selective breeding considered evidence for evolution?
options: It shows that species are fixed and unchanging
It proves natural selection has a goal
It creates new genes from nothing
It shows that heritable characteristics of a population can change substantially over generations
questions.explanation: Domesticated breeds differ greatly from their wild ancestors, showing that selection (artificial here) changes heritable traits over time, as natural selection does in the wild.

questions.prompt: What two processes are required for one species to split into two?
options: Reproductive isolation and differential selection
Mutation and selective breeding
Hybridization and extinction
Asexual reproduction and cloning
questions.explanation: Isolation stops gene flow; different selection pressures (and random changes) then make the populations diverge until they can no longer interbreed.

questions.statement: Speciation by splitting increases the total number of species.
questions.explanation: One species becomes two. Gradual change of a single species over time without splitting does not increase species number.

questions.prompt: Bonobos and chimpanzees are thought to have diverged after their ancestors were separated. What separated them?
options: A mountain range in East Africa
Different breeding seasons
The Congo River
Polyploidy in one population
questions.explanation: The Congo River formed a barrier that apes could not cross, so populations to the south (bonobos) and north (chimpanzees) were isolated and diverged.

questions.text: Separation that prevents populations from interbreeding is called reproductive ___.
questions.explanation: Once gene flow stops, changes in one population are no longer shared with the other.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of speciation by splitting.
items: A barrier stops gene flow between two groups
Different selection pressures act on each group
Allele frequencies diverge over many generations
The groups can no longer interbreed: two species
questions.explanation: Isolation must come first; differential selection then causes divergence until reproductive isolation is permanent.

questions.statement: Isolated populations will always become separate species, however short the separation.
questions.explanation: If the barrier disappears before enough divergence has occurred, the populations can interbreed again and merge.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Different selection pressures on separate populations

questions.explanation: Speciation results when reproductive isolation is combined with differential selection.

questions.prompt: Why does differential selection cause isolated populations to diverge?
options: Because isolation causes more mutations
Because different environments favour different alleles, changing allele frequencies in different directions
Because organisms choose to adapt to their environment
Because selection makes all populations identical
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on existing variation; different conditions favour different heritable traits, so the populations change in different ways.

questions.text: The formation of new species is called ___.
questions.explanation: Speciation, by splitting of an existing species, is the source of new biodiversity.

questions.prompt: Bonobos and chimpanzees can produce hybrids in captivity but are classed as separate species. What best explains this?
options: They have different numbers of chromosomes
They are in different genera
They do not interbreed in the wild because they are separated, and they differ in behaviour and anatomy
Hybrids are always impossible between species
questions.explanation: They have diverged in traits and are reproductively isolated in nature, showing why the boundary between populations and species can be difficult to define.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes allopatric from sympatric speciation?
options: Allopatric involves a geographical barrier; sympatric occurs in the same area
Allopatric only occurs in plants; sympatric only in animals
Sympatric speciation always needs a river or mountain
Allopatric speciation is always abrupt
questions.explanation: Both require reproductive isolation and lead to new species; they differ in whether the isolation is geographical (allopatric) or arises in the same place (sympatric).

questions.prompt: Match each isolating mechanism to its type of speciation.

pairs.left: Different mating rituals in one area
Breeding at different times of year

questions.explanation: Geographical barriers produce allopatric speciation; behavioural, temporal or polyploidy-based isolation within one area produces sympatric speciation.

questions.statement: A mule is sterile because the horse and donkey chromosomes cannot pair properly in meiosis.
questions.explanation: Horses have 64 and donkeys 62 chromosomes, so the mule has 63 unmatched chromosomes. Hybrid sterility prevents alleles mixing between the parent species.

questions.text: Rapid diversification of one ancestral species into many species adapted to different niches is called adaptive ___.
questions.explanation: Adaptive radiation, e.g. Darwin's finches on the Galápagos, creates biodiversity as species exploit different food sources and habitats.

questions.prompt: Which situation most often leads to adaptive radiation?
options: Two species hybridising to form a sterile offspring
A species colonising an area with many unoccupied niches
A population being reduced to very few individuals
Selective breeding of crop plants
questions.explanation: When few competitors are present (e.g. on newly formed islands), descendants of a colonist can diversify to fill many vacant niches.

questions.prompt: How can polyploidy cause abrupt speciation in plants?
options: Polyploid plants always die, removing alleles
Polyploidy makes plants reproduce only asexually
Polyploid plants cannot produce fertile offspring with the parent species, so they are instantly reproductively isolated
Polyploidy creates a geographical barrier
questions.explanation: Offspring of a tetraploid and a diploid would be triploid and sterile, so a polyploid is reproductively isolated in one generation, a form of sympatric speciation.

questions.prompt: Order the events in abrupt speciation by hybridization and polyploidy.
items: A sterile hybrid forms because chromosomes cannot pair
Chromosome number doubles in the hybrid
Each chromosome now has a partner, so meiosis works
A fertile, reproductively isolated new species exists
questions.explanation: Doubling gives every chromosome a homologue, restoring fertility while isolating the polyploid from both parents, as in knotweeds (Persicaria).

questions.statement: Sympatric speciation is generally slower than allopatric speciation because it always requires a physical barrier.
questions.explanation: Sympatric speciation does not require a physical barrier, and when caused by polyploidy it can be abrupt, occurring in a single generation.

questions.text: Having more than two sets of chromosomes is called ___.
questions.explanation: Polyploidy (e.g. 3n, 4n) is common in plants and is an important route to new plant species.

questions.prompt: Which is a barrier to hybridization that acts before fertilisation?
options: Hybrid sterility
Hybrid offspring dying young
Hybrid offspring being less fit
Different courtship behaviours so the species do not mate
questions.explanation: Behavioural, temporal and geographical barriers stop mating occurring. Hybrid sterility and low hybrid viability act after fertilisation.
